content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces DMAE, a knowledge distillation method for the pretrained Masked Autoencoders (MAE) models. In addition to the self-supervised MAE (i.e. reconstruction) loss, DMAE also learns to align the intermediate features of a pretrained teacher model and the target student model. DMAE is shown to be a more efficient knowledge distiller that could be trained with patches covering only 2% of the original image. The paper also shows that distilling from pretrained models + finetuning is a better paradigm for transfer learning, outperforming directly distilling from fine-tuned models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

**[S1]** Efficiency. With a pretrained MAE model as the teacher, DMAE can be trained efficiently with a high masking ratio (i.e. 98%). Distilling the knowledge of the intermediate features from the teacher model can further reduce the computation overhead.

**[S2]** Ablations and analysis of various experiment designs are provided, e.g. where to distill, masking ratio, extra prediction head, etc.

**[S3]** The writing is clear.

---

Weaknesses

**[W1]** The most interesting part of DMAE would be its efficiency. It is also the main claim of the paper. It would be better to include more experiments on this as currently it is only discussed in Sec. 4.6 (6 lines) and table 9, and the result is relatively weak: DMAE vs Supervised Feature Alignment: 195h vs 208h. There are potentially more things to be discussed, e.g. memory usage (DMAE seems to use less memory), FLOPS (fewer patches, fewer flops), etc. It is ok to include the comparisons between MAE and DMAE for completeness as in table 9. But it would be better to avoid claiming that DMAE outperforms MAE in accuracy and efficiency as it is misleading: DMAE requires a larger pretrained MAE model as the teacher, which is a huge overhead. With this overhead considered, DMAE shows no benefit in both accuracy (83.6 vs 84.0 in table 9) and efficiency.

**[W2]** Comparison between distilling from a pretrained model + finetuning (*distill+finetune*) and distilling from a finetuned model directly (*direct-distill*). 

Here I would prefer some clarifications from the authors: for the *direct-distill* baseline, would the student model be further finetuned on the target task after the knowledge distillation?

In general, I’m not sure if the comparison is sufficiently interesting as the *direct-distill* baseline may be infeasible:

* *direct-distill* has more overheads as it requires finetuning a large teacher. The obtained finetuned model may be of limited usefulness other than for distillation.

* *direct-distill* may not always be feasible as it may easily overfit if the downstream task has limited data.

* if *direct-distill* does not involve extra finetuning as in *distill+finetune*, the result is not surprising at all.

**[W3]** Other downstream tasks. DMAE is only evaluated on the ImageNet1K recognition. I believe evaluations on other downstream tasks are necessary, as in all the other self-supervised works. Benchmarks with limited annotations would be of great interest as the pretraining is crucial for such tasks. Again, for tasks with limited labels, *direct-distill* is not a reasonable baseline.

**[W4]** Literature: self-supervised knowledge distillation has been explored previously for lightweight student models:

* [1] CompRess: Self-Supervised Learning by Compressing Representations (NeurIPS 2020)
* [2] SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation (ICLR 2021)
* [3] SimReg: Regression as a Simple Yet Effective Tool for Self-supervised Knowledge Distillation (BMVC 2021)

DMAE shares some similar designs with these works. For example, SimReg also proposes to align the features instead of the soft-logits. SimReg also shows that using an extra prediction head can improve the downstream performance of the student model. I believe these works should be discussed and cited.

**[W5]** DMAE combines the reconstruction loss (L_{MAE}) and the distillation loss (L_{Dist}) (Eq. 3). To me, L_{Dist} provides stronger supervisions while L_{MAE} looks more like an extra regularization loss. I wonder if L_{MAE} is necessary at all in the knowledge distillation framework. A baseline with only L_{Dist} would be a good addition to the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is written clearly but further clarifications on the *direct-distill* baseline would be preferred [W2].
I believe the paper can be reproduced.
The technical contribution of the paper is weak though.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a new knowledge distillation method for the self-supervised MAE models. The proposed DMAE method is shown to be more efficient compared to other distillation approaches. The technical contributions and insights of DMAE are weak. I'm not sure if the contributions/novelties of this submission are sufficient to merit an ICLR paper. The paper could become stronger if more discussions about efficiency are included.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on conducting knowledge distillation. However, different from traditional distillation settings for supervised models, the proposed DMAE tries to perform knowledge distillation when the teacher is a self-supervised pre-trained model. By utilizing the asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture of MAE, the proposed DMAE architecture can perform knowledge distillation in a much more effective and efficient manner.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength:
  - This paper is well-organized with extensive experiments supporting the motivation.
  - The authors provide detailed analysis about the training time consumption of different baselines.
  - The proposed method is simple but effective. 

- Weakness:
  - To compare with MAE, it would be more interesting to utilize a 1600+100 epoch pre-trained MAE as instead of a 1600-epoch pre-trained baseline in Tab. 2, 7 and 8, which is the fair comparison according to effective computational cost.
  - To compare with other distillation methods, it would be more interesting to utilize MAE pre-training as initialization also for the baseline methods in Tab. 6, otherwise the time comparison in Tab. 9 is also unfair.
  - For representation learning works, it would be more interesting to report results on several downstream tasks, instead of just ImageNet classification, and more training lengths, instead of just 100 epoch distillation, to prevent over-fitting towards ImageNet validation.
  - To conclude, it seems that all the experiments conducted in this paper are taking a 1600-epoch pre-trained MAE, so-called "luxury" setups claimed by the authors in the last line of Page 1, for granted, which is not a fair way to support your motivation.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new knowledge distillation method for vision transformer, which the author name DMAE. For efficiency consideration, DMAE only proceeds a small visible subset of patches for the encoder to reduce the computational complexity and mimic the intermediate features of the teacher model so that only the first few layers of the teacher model need to be forward. Experimental results show that applying DMAE on the VIT-Base model gives 84.0 Top-1 accuracy with only 100 epochs of pretraining and fine-tuning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength** 
1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
2. DMAE is an efficient framework that reduces a lot of training costs for vision transformers.

**Weaknesses** 
1. This work is lack of novelty. Proceeds a small visible subset of patches for the encoder network is initially proposed in MAE, which I think cannot be regarded as a contribution of this paper. Mimic the intermediate features is also not a new technique in knowledge distillation. From my perspective, the only contribution of this paper is to forward only a few layers of the teacher model, which might slightly accelerate the training process. However, such a point is not enough to be accepted by ICLR.

2. Vision transformer always requires longer training epochs to get fully converged. Most papers in this research community will use 300 epochs as their default setting. However, this paper adopts only 100 epochs in their experiments and only compares DMAE with the 100 epochs results of other methods. In this case, we cannot ensure that all methods are fully converged. For example, the supervised setting for VIT-Tiny in Table 7 only achieves 66.6% Top-1 accuracy, which is far from the 300 epochs results (72.2%). Also, 100 epoch DMAE on VIT-Tiny obviously does not surpass this baseline. A more appropriate comparison should happen between longer training results. 

3. This paper claims that it focuses on distilling knowledge in the pre-training stage. However, pre-training aims to transfer the learned representations or whole network parameters into various downstream tasks. This is why many pre-training methods are often evaluated in various transfer learning scenarios. Nevertheless, this paper only evaluates their pre-trained method on classification tasks, which I think is insufficient to prove the superiority. I highly recommend the author provide more experimental results on various downstream tasks. For example, fine-tuning on downstream classification datasets, object detection, and semantic segmentation, which are evaluated in the original MAE paper.

4. Some important references are missing. A comparison with the most recent works [1,2] is desired.

[1] Meta Knowledge Distillation. 

[2] A Closer Look at Self-supervised Lightweight Vision Transformers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written, and I think it should be easy to reproduce the results. However, the limited novelty and inadequate experiments lower the quality of this paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new framework, DMAE, that introduces distillation operations into the MAE training process, achieving better performance on smaller models by using larger pre-trained models for guidance, while improving training efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Well written and easy to follow
- DMAE does show a high training efficiency compared to standard training of MAE.

Weaknesses
- This paper seems to just introduce the distillation operation into the MAE training process, and considering that the sparse operations all come from MAE, DMAE does not show any essential difference from the normal distillation operation. The interesting point, however, is whether this sparse distillation operation has a chance to be used as a general speedup rather than being restricted to MAE scenarios.
- In terms of pre-training, the most central issue is the transfer performance of the pre-trained models. From the experimental results, the distilled ViT-Base from ViT-Large only achieved slightly better results than direct pre-training by MAE. And the performance on more downstream tasks (e.g. COCO object detection, ADE-20K semantic segmentation) was also not demonstrated.
- A little confused about the relative positions of the teacher layers in Table 2. What does this mean when it refers to the Middle/Top/Bottom layers? A possible way to better present Section 4.2 might be to try every combination of several layers from layers 1-24 in the teacher model (e.g. ViT-Large) and several layers from layers 1-12 in the student model (e.g. ViT-Base) and show the results in one table?
- Notice in Table 3 that the MAE loss is always applied. Why not try to remove this part and turn it into a complete distillation framework?
- Poor performance on small models. As shown in Table 7, the results of ViT-Tiny/Small are even inferior to their supervised counterparts (DeiT-Ti 72.2, DeiT-S 79.8).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Good clarity and reproducibility.
- Please refer to the previous section for possible problems in quality and novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper attempts to introduce distillation operations into MAE and designs a new framework DMAE. However, DMAE does not show significant changes or special properties compared to standard distillation operation. Also, considering that the core issue of pre-trained models is the transfer performance, the lack of more downstream experiments, the slight improvements on ViT-B and even inferior performance on ViT-Ti/S further weaken the value of DMAE.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
